--- title: "Interaction Terms" subtitle: "When the effect of one variable depends on another" author: "Prof. Eric Friedlander" footer: "[🔗 MATH 2025 - Fall 2026 - Schedule](https://ericfriedlander.github.io/math2025-fa26/)" logo: "../images/logo.png" format: revealjs: theme: slides.scss multiplex: false transition: fade slide-number: false incremental: false chalkboard: true html-math-method: method: mathjax url: "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/mathjax@3/es5/tex-mml-chtml.js" execute: freeze: auto echo: true cache: false knitr: opts_chunk: R.options: width: 200 bibliography: references.bib --- # Review: AE 17 ## Where we are {.smaller} Last time we fit our first multiple regression on the coffee truck: `Sales` from `Temperature` **and** a categorical variable. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} |term | estimate| std.error| statistic| p.value| |:----------------|--------:|---------:|---------:|-------:| |(Intercept) | 116.93| 20.75| 5.64| 0.00| |Temperature | -0.72| 0.35| -2.07| 0.04| |LocationCityHall | -3.88| 4.24| -0.91| 0.36| |LocationPark | 11.48| 4.13| 2.78| 0.01| |LocationZoo | -17.39| 4.21| -4.13| 0.00| ::: ::: ::: question Interpret the `Temperature` coefficient and the `LocationZoo` coefficient. What does the fitted picture look like? ::: . . . - `Temperature`: holding `Location` constant, each extra °F is associated with about 0.72 fewer cups. - `LocationZoo`: holding `Temperature` constant, the Zoo sells about 17 fewer cups than the Business District. - The fitted picture is **parallel lines**: one slope, one intercept per location. # Prediction ## Prediction {.smaller} ::: question How many bikes do we expect on a 25°C summer day? ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} new_day <- tibble(temp_orig = 25, season = "summer") predict(mlr_fit, new_day) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 1 5041.681 ``` ::: ::: ## Cautions {.smaller} - **Do not extrapolate!** With several predictors you can extrapolate in many directions at once, even when each predictor is individually in range. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](18-interactions_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){fig-align='center' width=80%} ::: ::: ::: question Would you trust a prediction for a 30°C winter day? ::: ## Cautions {.smaller} - **Do not extrapolate!** With several predictors you can extrapolate in many directions at once, even when each predictor is individually in range. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](18-interactions_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){fig-align='center' width=80%} ::: ::: ::: question Would you trust a prediction for a 30°C winter day? ::: . . . - The model shows **association, not causation**. Season and temperature are tangled together in observational data. ## Activity: Parts 4-5 {.smaller} ::: appex 📋 [AE 17 - Multiple Linear Regression with the Coffee Truck](https://ericfriedlander.github.io/math2025-fa26/ae/ae-17-mlr-coffee-truck.html) ::: - Part 4: predict `Sales` for a new day, and find a prediction you should not trust. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ## From parallel lines to interactions {.smaller} Every model so far has been **additive**: the effect of one variable is the same at every value of the other. In a plot, that means **parallel lines**. ::: question Is it believable that an extra degree adds the same number of rentals in winter as in summer? That diabetes raises blood pressure by the same amount for men and for women? ::: . . . Today: 1. Conceptualizing models with two predictors. 2. Three cases, one picture each: **two categorical** (group means), **one of each** (lines), **two quantitative** (a surface). 3. **AE 18**. # Interaction Terms ## Interaction means multiplication {.smaller} With two explanatory variables $X_1$ and $X_2$, our model is purely additive. $$ \text{additive:}\quad \mu_Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \beta_2 X_2 $$ . . . Adding an interaction term, multiplies two variables, treating the product like a new variable: . . . $$ \text{with interaction:}\quad \mu_Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \beta_2 X_2 + \beta_3 X_1 X_2 $$ . . . Intuition: The impact of $X_1$ on $Y$, depends on the value of $X_2$ (and vice versa) # Case 1: Two categorical variables ## The data {.smaller} The Framingham Heart Study, as in Lectures 15 and 16. Our response is systolic blood pressure (`sysBP`, mm Hg). ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Rows: 4,240 Columns: 6 $ sysBP 106.0, 121.0, 127.5, 150.0, 130.0, 180.0, 138.0, 100.0… $ sex Male, Female, Male, Female, Female, Female, Female, Fe… $ diabetes_status Not diabetic, Not diabetic, Not diabetic, Not diabetic… $ age 39, 46, 48, 61, 46, 43, 63, 45, 52, 43, 50, 43, 46, 41… $ BMI 26.97, 28.73, 25.34, 28.58, 23.10, 30.30, 33.11, 21.68… $ totChol 195, 250, 245, 225, 285, 228, 205, 313, 260, 225, 254,… ``` ::: ::: - `sex`: Female or Male. - `diabetes_status`: Not diabetic or Diabetic. - `age` (years), `BMI`, and `totChol` (total cholesterol, mg/dL): we will use these later. ## Modeling blood pressure from sex and diabetes {.smaller} Let's start with what we know: an **additive** model with both predictors. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} add_fit <- lm(sysBP ~ diabetes_status + sex, data = fram) add_fit |> tidy() |> kable(digits = 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |term | estimate| std.error| statistic| p.value| |:-----------------------|--------:|---------:|---------:|-------:| |(Intercept) | 132.67| 0.45| 296.34| 0.00| |diabetes_statusDiabetic | 15.57| 2.12| 7.33| 0.00| |sexMale | -1.68| 0.68| -2.47| 0.01| ::: ::: This model says the effect of diabetes is **the same** for men and for women (and the male vs. female difference is the same whether or not someone has diabetes). ## How good is this model? {.smaller} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](18-interactions_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){fig-align='center' width=65%} ::: ::: ::: question Lines show the model's predicted mean for each group. Diamonds show the **actual** mean of each group. Does it look like the impact of diabetes depends on sex? ::: . . . ::: question How could the model be better? ::: ## What do the data say? {.smaller} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} |sex | Not diabetic| Diabetic| |:------|------------:|--------:| |Female | 132.5| 153.9| |Male | 131.2| 140.3| ::: ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](18-interactions_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){fig-align='center' width=65%} ::: ::: ::: question Does diabetes change blood pressure by the same amount for men and for women? ::: ## It depends! {.smaller} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: - **Women:** diabetes goes with a blood pressure about 21 mm Hg higher. - **Men:** diabetes goes with a blood pressure about 9 mm Hg higher. . . . When the effect of `diabetes_status` **depends on** `sex`, we say there is an **interaction** between `diabetes_status` and `sex`. # The interaction model ## Adding an interaction {.smaller} To let the diabetes effect differ by sex, we add the **product** of the indicator variables: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} int_fit <- lm(sysBP ~ diabetes_status * sex, data = fram) int_fit |> tidy() |> kable(digits = 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |term | estimate| std.error| statistic| p.value| |:-------------------------------|--------:|---------:|---------:|-------:| |(Intercept) | 132.54| 0.45| 294.63| 0.00| |diabetes_statusDiabetic | 21.40| 2.93| 7.30| 0.00| |sexMale | -1.35| 0.69| -1.97| 0.05| |diabetes_statusDiabetic:sexMale | -12.26| 4.25| -2.88| 0.00| ::: ::: `diabetes_status * sex` is shorthand for `diabetes_status + sex + diabetes_status:sex` where the color specifies an interaction term. ## The model equation {.smaller} With the reference levels Not diabetic and Female: $$ \begin{aligned} \widehat{\text{sysBP}} = &\hat\beta_0 \\ &+ \hat\beta_1 \,\text{Diabetic} + \hat\beta_2 \,\text{Male} \\ &\underbrace{+ \hat\beta_3 \,(\text{Diabetic} \times \text{Male})}_{\text{interaction term}} \end{aligned} $$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: $$ \begin{aligned} \widehat{\text{sysBP}} = &132.5 \\ &+21.4 \,\text{Diabetic} -1.4 \,\text{Male} \\ &\underbrace{-12.3 \,(\text{Diabetic} \times \text{Male})}_{\text{interaction term}} \end{aligned} $$ ::: question For each of the four combinations of diabetes status and sex, which terms are "on"? Write the equation for each one. ::: ## Recovering the cell means {.smaller} Each of the four means is the sum of the terms that are "on": ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} |Combination |Terms on | Model value| |:--------------------|:-----------------|-----------:| |Female, Not diabetic |b0 | 132.5| |Female, Diabetic |b0 + b1 | 153.9| |Male, Not diabetic |b0 + b2 | 131.2| |Male, Diabetic |b0 + b1 + b2 + b3 | 140.3| ::: ::: . . . The interaction model reproduces all four means exactly. It has one parameter per cell. ## Interpreting the interaction term {.smaller} :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="45%"} - $\hat\beta_0$: the mean for the reference group, **non-diabetic women**. - $\hat\beta_1$ (`diabetes_statusDiabetic`): the diabetes effect **for women** (the reference sex). It is *not* the overall diabetes effect anymore. - $\hat\beta_2$ (`sexMale`): Male minus Female **among non-diabetic participants** (the reference diabetes status). - $\hat\beta_3$ (`diabetes_statusDiabetic:sexMale`): how much **bigger** (or smaller) the diabetes effect is for men than for women. The **gap** between the dotted line (men if the lines were parallel) and the actual men's mean. ::: ::: {.column width="55%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](18-interactions_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-15-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: :::: ::: question Use the coefficients to find the Male minus Female difference among participants with diabetes. Does it match the table of means we saw earlier? ::: # Case 2: Categorical-Quantitative Interaction ## Is the age slope the same for men and women? {.smaller} Now let's predict `sysBP` from `age` and `sex`. An additive model gives one slope for age and a different intercept for each sex. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](18-interactions_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-16-1.png){fig-align='center' width=80%} ::: ::: ::: question Do we believe that men and women age in the same way? ::: ## Letting the slope depend on sex {.smaller} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](18-interactions_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-17-1.png){fig-align='center' width=80%} ::: ::: ::: question Which group's blood pressure rises faster with age? At what age do the lines nearly meet? ::: ## Slopes by sex {.smaller} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} age_int |> tidy() |> kable(digits = 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |term | estimate| std.error| statistic| p.value| |:-----------|--------:|---------:|---------:|-------:| |(Intercept) | 66.37| 2.39| 27.79| 0| |age | 1.34| 0.05| 28.33| 0| |sexMale | 37.07| 3.64| 10.19| 0| |age:sexMale | -0.77| 0.07| -10.64| 0| ::: ::: - Women (the reference level): slope $\hat\beta_1$ = 1.34 mm Hg per year. - Men: slope $\hat\beta_1 + \hat\beta_3$ = 0.57 mm Hg per year. ::: question What does the negative interaction coefficient say about how blood pressure changes with age for men compared with women? ::: # Case 3: Two quantitative ## Age and BMI {.smaller} Finally, two quantitative predictors. Let's predict total cholesterol (`totChol`, mg/dL) from: - $X_1$ = `age` (years), $X_2$ = `BMI`. $$ \widehat{\text{totChol}} = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 \,\text{age} + \hat\beta_2 \,\text{BMI} + \hat\beta_3 \,(\text{age} \times \text{BMI}) $$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} quant_add <- lm(totChol ~ age + BMI, data = fram) quant_int <- lm(totChol ~ age * BMI, data = fram) # the 3D pictures show 600 randomly chosen participants (plotting all 4,000+ is slow) set.seed(2026) fram_pts <- fram |> drop_na(totChol, BMI) |> filter(totChol < 400, BMI < 45) |> slice_sample(n = 600) quant_xs <- seq(min(fram$age), max(fram$age), length.out = 30) quant_ys <- seq(17, 40, length.out = 30) quant_labels <- c("Age (years)", "BMI", "Total cholesterol") ``` ::: ## Additive: a flat plane {.smaller} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: The age slope is $\hat\beta_1 =$ 1.33 mg/dL per year for **every** BMI. ## Interaction: a twisted surface {.smaller} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ::: question Compare the edge where BMI is low with the edge where BMI is high. Along which edge does cholesterol rise faster with age? ::: ## The slope is now a function {.smaller} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} quant_int |> tidy() |> kable(digits = 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |term | estimate| std.error| statistic| p.value| |:-----------|--------:|---------:|---------:|-------:| |(Intercept) | -5.860| 24.361| -0.241| 0.81| |age | 4.406| 0.482| 9.139| 0.00| |BMI | 6.873| 0.938| 7.324| 0.00| |age:BMI | -0.119| 0.018| -6.470| 0.00| ::: ::: $$ \text{slope of age} = \hat\beta_1 + \hat\beta_3 \times \text{BMI} $$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} | BMI| Slope of age| |---:|------------:| | 21| 1.90| | 25| 1.42| | 31| 0.71| ::: ::: . . . For a fixed BMI, the slope of age is a number. As BMI changes, the slope changes **linearly**: that is what a product term does. ::: question Interpret $\hat\beta_3$: how does the age slope change for each one-unit increase in BMI? ::: ## An interaction we don't need {.smaller} Not every pair of quantitative variables interacts. What about age and cholesterol for predicting blood pressure? ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} |term | estimate| std.error| statistic| p.value| |:-----------|--------:|---------:|---------:|-------:| |(Intercept) | 71.5948| 9.9440| 7.1998| 0.0000| |age | 0.9577| 0.2001| 4.7861| 0.0000| |totChol | 0.0614| 0.0424| 1.4453| 0.1484| |age:totChol | -0.0001| 0.0008| -0.1262| 0.8995| ::: ::: ::: question The interaction coefficient is tiny relative to its standard error, and the age slope is about the same at every cholesterol level. What would the surface look like? Would you add the term? ::: # The three cases ## Same idea, three pictures {.smaller} | | Two categorical | One of each | Two quantitative | |:---|:---|:---|:---| | Example | `diabetes_status` x `sex` | `age` x `sex` | `age` x `BMI` | | Picture | jitter plot with group means | scatterplot with fitted lines | 3D surface | | Additive model | same gap between groups at every level (parallel profiles) | parallel lines | flat tilted plane | | Interaction adds | the 4th corner (a twist) | a different slope per group | a slope that changes with $X_2$ | | $\hat\beta_3$ means | difference in differences | the **change in slope** from the reference group | change in the slope of $X_1$ per unit of $X_2$ | . . . In all three cases, the interaction term is $X_1 \times X_2$, and it is what **bends** the surface. # Choosing a model ## Do we need the interaction? {.smaller} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} |model | r.squared| sigma| |:---------------------|---------:|-----:| |BP: diabetes + sex | 0.014| 21.9| |BP: diabetes * sex | 0.016| 21.9| |BP: age + sex | 0.156| 20.2| |BP: age * sex | 0.178| 20.0| |Chol: age + BMI | 0.077| 42.9| |Chol: age * BMI | 0.086| 42.6| |BP: age + cholesterol | 0.166| 20.1| |BP: age * cholesterol | 0.166| 20.1| ::: ::: ::: question Which interaction is worth adding? How do you know? (Think about $R^2$, $\hat{\sigma}_\epsilon$, and the pictures.) ::: . . . - A real interaction should show up in the plot, the $R^2$, and the size of the interaction coefficients relative to $\hat{\sigma}_\epsilon$. - Every interaction adds parameters. Add one when the picture and the context call for it. - We will learn formal tools for this later. ## Interactions and "holding constant" {.smaller} Last time: a coefficient is the change in the mean response per unit change in that predictor, **holding the other predictors constant**. . . . With an interaction, that sentence is incomplete: - There is **no single** effect of diabetes. There is one for women and one for men. - Always describe the effect **at a particular value** of the other variable. . . . ::: question A patient asks, "How much does diabetes raise my blood pressure?" What should you say back? ::: ## Activity: AE 18 {.smaller} ::: appex 📋 [AE 18 - Interactions with the Coffee Truck](https://ericfriedlander.github.io/math2025-fa26/ae/ae-18-interactions-coffee-truck.html) ::: - Each group gets a different pair of locations. - Build the table of means, plot the interaction, and fit both the additive and interaction models. - Recommend where Jo should park for each shift. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ## Recap {.smaller} - An **interaction** means the effect of one variable depends on the value of another. - Categorical x categorical: the interaction terms are "differences in differences". - Categorical x quantitative: each group gets its own slope (parallel lines become non-parallel). - Quantitative x quantitative: the slope of one variable changes **linearly** with the other. - Geometrically, an additive model is a **flat plane** and an interaction **twists** it. - With an interaction, main effects are the effects at the reference level, not overall effects. - An additive model can hide a big pattern. Plot the data first. . . . **Next time:** we have a lot of estimates, like "City Hall sells 18 more cups at Lunch". How sure are we? **Confidence intervals.**

  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1

      });

  })();
</script>
